newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-DEFENDER JONES HAPPY TO BE IN BACKGROUND AT OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-DEFENDER JONES HAPPY TO BE IN BACKGROUND AT OPEN.

text.p: Defending champion Steve Jones does not begrudge the buzz surrounding Tiger Woods at the U.S. Open.
The young Masters champion draws a whirlwind of attention wherever he goes at Congressional Country Club, while Jones goes about his business in anonymity.
But the 38-year-old Jones likes life outside the spotlight and relishes the chance to live out his Cinderella story all over again when the championship starts on Thursday.

"I don't play golf to get attention," Jones told an interview room gathering of about 50 scattered reporters directly after a mob some 10 times larger had squeezed in to hear from Masters champion Woods.
"If there was a way just to play golf and not have the attention part of it, that would be fine by me."
Jones, in fact, is a big fan of Woods, the 21-year-old winner of five tournaments on the U.S. tour in nine months since turning pro.
"Tiger is a phenom," Jones said about the young man who set Augusta National agog as he crushed the elite field by 12 strokes.
"That guy is a young superstar. He's a phenom. He's letting his clubs do the talking. The guy is awesome. What can I say? He's getting what he deserves."
Jones deservedly won his Open title last year in a final- round duel at Oakland Hills with good friend Tom Lehman, who assuaged his disappointment by winning the British Open one month later.

"I had no idea how special or what a thrill it was until a year has gone by," Jones said about winning his first major. "It has been the greatest thrill of my golfing career. That moment will never be recreated."

The one-stroke victory over Lehman and Davis Love capped an inspiring comeback story for Jones, who missed three years on tour after suffering ligament and joint damage to his left ring finger after a 1991 dirt bike accident.

This year, Jones started fast with a tie for sixth at the Mercedes champonship, a tie for ninth at the Bob Hope and victory at the Phoenix Open. He added a second-place finish at the Tucson Open before his game mysteriously left him.
Jones has missed five cuts in the last eight tournaments and tied for 47th and 60th in his last two outings.
Still, he sees hope in the way he is now striking the ball.
"I hit the ball probably the best I've ever hit it in my career last week," said Jones, who faulted his course management and putting for his poor Kemper Open result.
"I'd love to repeat. That's definitely a goal of mine. It's not out of reach by no means. I know if I hit the ball decent and putt well I've got a shot.
"I'm Cinderella again this week, which is fine by me."
